senses: One who specializes in endodontics, a specialty of dentistry.
ety: From endo- (“within”) + -odont (“tooth”) + -ist (“specialist”).
examples: Her father is an endodontist and her mother is an interior and architectural designer.

senses: A gateway consisting of two upright pillars carrying one to three transverse lintels, often minutely carved with symbolic sculpture, and serving as a monumental approach to a Buddhist temple.
ety: Borrowed from Sanskrit तोरण (toraṇa, “arched portal”).

senses: The treatment of cardiac arrhythmia, either with medication or by use of a machine (a cardioverter) that delivers a controlled electric current.
ety: From cardio- (“heart”) + -version (“changing”). Compare reversion and conversion.
examples: The posologies employed require careful clinical and electrical supervision, and the same anticoagulant measures as for electrical cardioversion are necessary.

senses: In Ancient Greek mythology, a kind of spectre sent by Hecate to guard roads and devour travellers.
ety: Ancient Greek Ἔμπουσα (Émpousa)

senses: Having or resembling a bloom (as on fruit).
Full of blooms; flowering.
ety: By surface analysis, bloom + -y. Cognate with Dutch bloemig, German blumig, Swedish blommig.

senses: A motorcycle taxi.
ety: 1990s, from the now defunct Nigerian airline, Okada Air, nicknamed so because they could manoeuvre through the heavy traffic of Lagos and take passengers to their destinations in a timely manner, in the same way as the airline. Originates from the Ẹ̀dó town of Okada.
examples: By the glittering blue lagoon, I stood next to the main ring road to flag down a motorcycle taxi, or okada. Okadas are the scourge of Nigeria's roads.

senses: That which neutralizes.
ety: From neutralize + -er.

senses: Resembling or characteristic of a marshmallow.
Soft and fluffy.
Tending to be a pushover; overly accommodating.
ety: From marshmallow + -y.
examples: I can only guess at Wavy Gravy I scream. I suspect it's a version of heavenly hash, which is a marshmallowier version of rocky road.
Percy struck some of the people who worked with him as an ineffective legislator, marshmallowy and yielding in the way of many moderate politicians.

senses: A spiritual or divine being in Ainu mythology, similar to the Japanese kami.
ety: From Ainu カムイ (kamuy).

senses: Sparkling intermittently.
ety: From Middle English twynkelynge, equivalent to twinkle + -ing.

senses: That squirms, writhes or wriggles.
ety: From squirm + -y.

senses: Causing or liable to cause inflation.
ety: From inflation + -ary.
examples: The rapid influx of precious metals from the new mines had an inflationary effect on the specie based economy.

senses: Characteristic of, or suitable to, a lawyer.
ety: From lawyer + -ly (adjectival suffix).
examples: She rewrote the letter to make it sound more lawyerly.
Norton had made a neat, lawyerly check beside each of the items he and Billy had picked up—half a dozen or so, including the milk and a six-pack of Coke.

senses: A drink made from rum, water, sugar, and nutmeg.
ety: Perhaps from Italian (baby-talk) bombo (“drink”), of imitative origin.

senses: The doctrine that all actions are determined by the current state and immutable laws of the universe, with no possibility of choice.
ety: Borrowed from French déterminisme, equivalent to determine + -ism.

senses: A ball of fluff.
A soft, fluffy, or round creature.
ety: From fluff + ball.
examples: The smallest of the Northern breeds, the Pomeranian is a four-legged fluffball with its thick double coat, small pointed ears, and bushy curled tail up over its back.

senses: A rural, unsophisticated person; a bumpkin.
A mangelwurzel.
ety: From German Wurzel (“root”), via mangelwurzel, a root crop cultivated for livestock feed beginning in the 18th century.

senses: A student or expert in sinology.
ety: From sinology (“study of China”) + -ist (“(agent)”). Equivalent to sino- (“China”) + -logist (“student of, expert on”).

senses: A person who kneels.
An apparatus that permits the loading door of a bus to decrease in height in order to facilitate boarding of passengers that are seniors and physically disadvantaged
On a gable end, the stone (often decorated) at the base of the slope of the gable on either side.
ety: From Middle English knelere, equivalent to kneel + -er.
examples: All the kneelers sighed with relief when they were told it was over and they could finally stand up.

senses: Synonym of torque (“collar or necklace of twisted metal”).
ety: Borrowed from Latin torquēs.
examples: The torqueses worn by their chiefs, and which were displayed as valuable trophies at Rome, were exquisite works of art, as is proved by such as have been dug up from time to time.

senses: The state of being indivisible, incapable of being divided.
An indivisible factor or object.
ety: From Middle French indivisibilité, from Ecclesiastical Latin indivisibilitas.

senses: A philosophy favouring the use of science and technology, especially neurotechnology, biotechnology, and nanotechnology, to overcome human limitations and improve the human condition.
ety: From trans- + humanism, coined by British evolutionary biologist, philosopher, author Julian Huxley in 1957.

senses: A light paper used as interleaving between artworks or stamp album pages.
Smooth, non-absorbing, grease- and moisture-resistant, supercalendered paper.
A small stamp packet made from glassine paper.
ety: From glass + -ine.
examples: Each illustration was protected by a glassine page that had to be turned delicately.

senses: Any of several varieties of the herb Perilla frutescens, related to basil and mint, used in Japanese cooking.
ety: From Japanese 紫蘇 (shiso).

senses: A hermit who lived in a tree.
ety: From Ancient Greek δενδρίτης (dendrítēs, “of or pertaining to a tree”). Equivalent to dendr- + -ite.

senses: A traditional Japanese toy with an attached ball that can be caught in any of three cups or on a spike.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese けん玉 (けんだま, kendama), from 拳 (けん, ken, “game played with the hands; fist”) or 剣 (けん, ken, “sword”) + 玉 (たま, tama, “ball”).

senses: To unregister.
To unsubscribe.
ety: From de- + register.

senses: Not readily communicated.
ety: From non- + communicable.

senses: Spit, usually frothy and of a milky coloration.
Something frothy and white that resembles spit.
Spit-up or drool of an infant.
ety: Alteration of dialectal spattle (by association with spit (noun)), from Old English spātl, which is related to spǣtan (whence spit (verb)).

senses: The theory that a mental state is identical to the disposition or tendency to behave in accordance with the physical causes; statements about the mind are reducible to statements of physical behavior.
ety: From behavior + -ism.
examples: Supporters of behaviorism claim that to be "in pain" is nothing more than the tendency to wince, yelp, scream "ouch!" and so on.
A traditional objection to behaviorism was that behaviorism could not be right because a system could behave as if it were conscious without actually being conscious.

senses: One who farms or hunts rabbits professionally; the keeper of a warren
ety: From Middle English warenner, warner, from Anglo-Norman warennier, variant of garennier; equivalent to warren + -er.

senses: The agricultural ecology
ety: From agro- + ecology.

senses: a prince in feudal Mongolia
commander of tumens and mingghans, military units of 10,000 and 1,000 soldiers respectively
ety: Borrowed from Classical Mongolian ᠨᠣᠶ᠋ᠠᠨ (noyan) and Middle Mongol [Term?].

senses: A king of ancient Mali.
ety: Borrowed from Eastern Maninkakan mànsa (“king”) and other related languages.

senses: An administrative subdivision in northern English counties, developed under Norse influence, and corresponding to hundreds in the rest of England.
ety: From Middle English wapentake, wepentake, wapentache, wapentac, from Old English wǣpenġetæc, from Old Norse vápnatak, from vápn (“weapon”) + taka (“take”), equivalent to weapon + take.

senses: The process of transferring decorative designs onto surfaces using decals.
ety: Borrowed from French décalcomanie.

senses: A popular style of folk music from Colombia.
A piece performed in this style.
ety: From Spanish vallenato, from valle (“valley”) nato (“born”).

senses: The progressive destruction of bone or tooth by decay.
ety: Borrowed from Latin cariēs.

senses: The metal griddle used in the teppanyaki style of Japanese cuisine.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 鉄板 (teppan, “iron plate”).

senses: A parlour game played in teams with three dice, originating in England but popular among suburban women in the United States at the beginning of the 21st century.
ety: Reportedly from Spanish banca, a card game.
